title: US/AZ Government & Constitution (12th Grade)
description: US and Arizona government, Constitution, and civics for 12th grade

questions.question: How many branches of the US government are there?
questions.explanation: The Constitution creates three branches - legislative, executive, and judicial - so no single group holds all the power.
questions.memoryHook: Three branches like three toes on my foot - legislative, executive, judicial!

questions.question: Which branch of government makes the laws?
questions.explanation: Article I gives Congress the power to make federal laws.
questions.memoryHook: Congress legislates - legislate starts with L, and so does laws!

questions.question: Which branch of government enforces the laws?
questions.explanation: Article II puts the President in charge of carrying out and enforcing federal laws.
questions.memoryHook: The executive executes - like executing a perfect dance move!

questions.question: Which branch of government interprets the laws?
questions.explanation: Article III creates the courts, and judges decide what laws mean when there is a dispute.
questions.memoryHook: Judges judge - the judicial branch is full of judges!

questions.question: What is the elected body that governs each Arizona county?
questions.explanation: Article 12, Section 3 of the Arizona Constitution creates the elected county offices, including at least three supervisors chosen by the voters for four-year terms. Boards of three or five supervisors set county policy and budgets and oversee services such as roads, jails, parks, and public health.
questions.memoryHook: Every county has a Board of Supervisors running the show - think of it as the county's own city council!

questions.question: What are the first ten amendments to the Constitution called?
questions.explanation: The first ten amendments were added in 1791 to protect individual freedoms, and together they are called the Bill of Rights.
questions.memoryHook: Ten amendments, ten tiny teeth - the Bill of Rights bites back against unfair government!

questions.question: Who is the chief law enforcement officer of an Arizona county?
distractors: The chief of the state highway patrol
questions.explanation: Article 12, Section 3 of the Arizona Constitution makes the sheriff an elected county officer with a four-year term. Sheriffs police unincorporated areas of the county, run the county jail, and serve court orders. The county attorney is a different elected officer - the county's prosecutor, not its police chief.
questions.memoryHook: The sheriff wears the badge for the whole county - and the voters, not the governor, hand out that badge!

questions.question: How many members are in the US House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: The House has 435 voting members, with seats divided among the states based on population.
questions.memoryHook: 435 representatives - imagine 435 people trying to fit in one room!

questions.question: How many senators are in the US Senate?
questions.explanation: Each of the 50 states elects 2 senators, making 100 total.
questions.memoryHook: 50 states times 2 senators - anyone can do that math: 100!

questions.question: How long is one term for a US Representative?
questions.explanation: House members serve two-year terms, so voters get a say about them very often.
questions.memoryHook: Two years - representatives have to run again before I finish a nap!

questions.question: How long is one term for a US Senator?
questions.explanation: Senators serve six-year terms, longer than House members, so the Senate changes more slowly.
questions.memoryHook: Six years is three times two - senators get three times the nap time!

questions.question: How long is a US presidential term?
questions.explanation: The President serves a four-year term and can be re-elected once.
questions.memoryHook: Four years - one term is a whole presidential childhood!

questions.question: What is the maximum number of terms a President can serve?
questions.explanation: The 22nd Amendment limits the President to two elected terms.
questions.memoryHook: Two terms max - even the President has to share the toys!

questions.question: What is the minimum voting age in US federal elections?
questions.explanation: The 26th Amendment lowered the voting age to 18 nationwide.
questions.memoryHook: 18 to vote - old enough to drive, old enough to pick the President!

questions.question: What is the capital of Arizona?
questions.explanation: Phoenix has been Arizona's capital since before statehood.
questions.memoryHook: Phoenix - the capital rises in the desert like its namesake bird from the ashes!

questions.question: The first three words of the Constitution are...?
questions.explanation: The Preamble begins 'We the People,' showing that government power comes from the citizens.
questions.memoryHook: We the People - every person is part of the people!

questions.question: Which amendment protects freedom of speech?
questions.explanation: The 1st Amendment protects speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition.
questions.memoryHook: First place for free speech - the 1st Amendment is number one!

questions.question: Which amendment protects the right to bear arms?
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights, the 2nd Amendment protects an individual right to own firearms, recognized by the Supreme Court in District of Columbia v. Heller (2008).
questions.memoryHook: Two arms for the 2nd Amendment - well, I have two tiny ones!

questions.question: Who is the head of the executive branch?
questions.explanation: Article II makes the President the chief executive who leads the executive branch.
questions.memoryHook: The President presides - that is why they call him President!

questions.question: What is the highest court in the United States?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court is the top of the federal court system and its decisions are final.
questions.memoryHook: Supreme means top - like the top of the food chain!

questions.question: Arizona's constitution was drafted at a convention in 1910. In what year did it take effect, when Arizona became a state?
questions.explanation: Delegates drafted the constitution at Phoenix in late 1910 and the people ratified it on February 9, 1911, but it became the law only on February 14, 1912, when President Taft proclaimed Arizona the 48th state. Arizona had been a territory since 1863.
questions.memoryHook: Arizona's constitution got a Valentine - it took effect on statehood day, February 14, 1912!

questions.question: Which house of Congress has the power to impeach a President?
questions.explanation: The House votes on articles of impeachment, which is like an official accusation; the Senate then holds the trial.
questions.memoryHook: The House impeaches - the House points the finger!

questions.question: What does the Vice President do in the Senate?
questions.correctAnswer: Serves as President of the Senate and breaks tie votes
questions.explanation: The Vice President presides over the Senate and votes only to break a tie.
questions.memoryHook: The VP is the tie-breaker - like breaking a tie in tug-of-war!

questions.question: Arizona was admitted to the Union as which state?
questions.explanation: Arizona became the 48th state on February 14, 1912.
questions.memoryHook: 48th state - Arizona was almost last to the party, but it brought the sunshine!

questions.question: How long is an Arizona governor's term?
questions.explanation: Arizona's governor is elected to a four-year term.
questions.memoryHook: Four years - same as the President, but with more cacti!

questions.question: What document is the supreme law of the land?
questions.explanation: Article VI says the Constitution is the supreme law, so no state law can override it.
questions.memoryHook: Supreme law - the Constitution wears the crown!

questions.question: Which amendment abolished slavery?
questions.explanation: The 13th Amendment, ratified in 1865, ended slavery in the United States.
questions.memoryHook: 13 ended slavery - unlucky 13 became lucky for freedom!

questions.question: Which amendment gave women the right to vote?
questions.explanation: The 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920, guaranteed women's suffrage.
questions.memoryHook: 19 for the women's vote - the 19th Amendment opened the ballot box for all!

questions.question: The Constitution opens with the words 'We the People.' This expresses popular sovereignty, the idea that government power comes from...?
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty means the people themselves are the source of all government authority. By beginning 'We the People of the United States... do ordain and establish this Constitution,' the framers claimed power from the people's consent - the same idea the Declaration of Independence called 'the consent of the governed.'
questions.memoryHook: 'We the People' means the power starts with people like you - not with kings, courts, or presidents!

questions.question: Powers shared by both federal and state governments are called...?
questions.explanation: Concurrent powers, like taxing, are exercised by both levels of government at the same time.
questions.memoryHook: Concurrent means together - like a duet!

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution establishes the legislative branch?
questions.explanation: Article I creates Congress and lists its powers.
questions.memoryHook: Article One is number one - the legislature comes first!

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution establishes the executive branch?
questions.explanation: Article II creates the presidency and describes the President's powers.
questions.memoryHook: Article Two - the President's article, the second branch in line!

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution establishes the judicial branch?
questions.explanation: Article III creates the Supreme Court and the federal court system.
questions.memoryHook: Article Three for the three levels of courts!

questions.question: What is the minimum age to serve in the House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: The Constitution requires House members to be at least 25 years old.
questions.memoryHook: 25 to join the House - you need a quarter-century of wisdom!

questions.question: What is the minimum age to serve in the Senate?
questions.explanation: Senators must be at least 30 years old under the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: 30 for the Senate - the Senate likes them a little older!

questions.question: What is the minimum age to be President?
questions.explanation: The President must be at least 35, a natural-born citizen, and a US resident for 14 years.
questions.memoryHook: 35 to be President - 35 is 30 plus 5, older than a senator!

questions.question: How many years must a House member have been a US citizen?
questions.explanation: The Constitution requires seven years of citizenship for the House.
questions.memoryHook: Seven years - lucky seven for the House!

questions.question: How many years must a Senator have been a US citizen?
questions.explanation: Senators need nine years of US citizenship, two more than House members.
questions.memoryHook: Nine years - senators need two more years than House members!

questions.question: Which amendment requires a speedy and public trial?
questions.explanation: The 6th Amendment guarantees a speedy public trial, an impartial jury, and the right to a lawyer.
questions.memoryHook: Six for speedy - the 6th Amendment does not let trials drag on!

questions.question: Which amendment protects against self-incrimination?
questions.explanation: The 5th Amendment says no one must testify against themselves - this is called 'pleading the Fifth.'
questions.memoryHook: Plead the Fifth - one amendment, a whole hand of protections: silence, due process, and more!

questions.question: Which amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures?
questions.explanation: The 4th Amendment requires warrants based on probable cause for searches and seizures.
questions.memoryHook: Four walls of your home - the 4th Amendment keeps them private!

questions.question: Which amendment bans cruel and unusual punishment?
questions.explanation: The 8th Amendment forbids cruel and unusual punishments and excessive bail.
questions.memoryHook: Eight is enough - the 8th Amendment says punishments cannot be cruel!

questions.question: What can Congress do if the President vetoes a bill?
questions.correctAnswer: Override the veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses
distractors: Ask the Supreme Court to cancel the veto
questions.explanation: Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds majority in the House and Senate, turning the bill into law anyway.
questions.memoryHook: Two-thirds overrides - Congress gets the last stomp!

questions.question: Who confirms Supreme Court justices?
questions.explanation: The President nominates justices, but the Senate must confirm them by majority vote.
questions.memoryHook: The Senate says yes - no justice without Senate permission!

questions.question: Phoenix uses the council-manager form of city government. In that system, who runs the city's day-to-day operations?
questions.correctAnswer: A professional city manager appointed by the mayor and city council
distractors: The mayor, acting as the city's chief executive
The Maricopa County Board of Supervisors
A city clerk chosen in a citywide election
questions.explanation: Phoenix is the largest city in the United States with council-manager government. The elected mayor and council set policy and pass the budget, then appoint a professional city manager to run daily operations and carry out their decisions. In a strong-mayor system, by contrast, the elected mayor personally serves as chief executive.
questions.memoryHook: In Phoenix the council sets the playbook and hires a pro manager to run the game - like owners hiring a coach!

questions.question: How many members are in the Arizona State Senate?
questions.explanation: Arizona has 30 legislative districts, and each district elects one senator, for 30 total.
questions.memoryHook: 30 senators for 30 districts - neat and tidy like my fossil collection!

questions.question: How many members are in the Arizona House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: Arizona has 30 districts, and each district elects two representatives, for 60 total.
questions.memoryHook: 60 representatives - double the senators, double the fun!

questions.question: Which Arizona process lets voters propose new laws directly?
questions.explanation: Arizona's initiative process lets citizens gather signatures to put a proposed law on the ballot.
questions.memoryHook: Initiative means you start it - citizens take the initiative!

questions.question: Which Arizona process lets voters approve or reject laws passed by the legislature?
questions.explanation: A referendum puts a recently passed law before voters to accept or reject it.
questions.memoryHook: Referendum refers it back - the people get the final roar!

questions.question: Which Arizona process lets voters remove an elected official before their term ends?
questions.explanation: Arizona voters can petition for a recall election to remove an official early.
questions.memoryHook: Recall means call back - voters call the official back home!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Electoral College?
questions.correctAnswer: The group of electors who formally elect the President
distractors: The committee that writes the Constitution
questions.explanation: Each state has electors equal to its House members plus senators; they cast the official votes for President.
questions.memoryHook: The Electoral College elects - 538 electors pick the President!

questions.question: How many electoral votes are needed to win the presidency?
questions.explanation: A candidate needs a majority of the 538 electoral votes, which is 270.
questions.memoryHook: 270 to win - more than half of 538, that is the magic number!

questions.question: Which amendment guarantees equal protection under the law?
questions.explanation: The 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause requires states to treat people equally.
questions.memoryHook: 14 for fairness - the 14th Amendment makes everyone equal!

questions.question: Which amendment protects voting rights regardless of race?
questions.explanation: The 15th Amendment says the right to vote cannot be denied based on race.
questions.memoryHook: 15 for every race - the 15th Amendment opens the ballot box to all!

questions.question: Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states by which amendment?
questions.explanation: The 10th Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people.
questions.memoryHook: Ten keeps the rest - the 10th Amendment saves powers for the states!

questions.question: Which statement best describes a 'special district' in Arizona local government?
questions.correctAnswer: A separate local government created to provide one specific service, such as fire protection, water, or irrigation
distractors: The part of a city represented by one city council member
A county that contains more than one city
A district drawn for electing members of the state legislature
questions.explanation: Special districts are single-purpose governments: fire districts, water and irrigation districts, and hospital districts each have their own elected board, budget, and power to charge fees or levy taxes for that one service. The area that elects a single council member is called a council district, which is not a separate government.
questions.memoryHook: A special district does ONE job - a fire district exists for fires, a water district for water, and that is it!

questions.question: What happens if no presidential candidate wins a majority of electoral votes?
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives chooses the President
distractors: The Supreme Court chooses the President
There is a national popular revote
questions.explanation: The 12th Amendment sends the election to the House, which votes by state delegation.
questions.memoryHook: The House decides - 50 states, 50 votes, one President!

questions.question: How many justices are on the Arizona Supreme Court?
questions.explanation: Arizona's highest court has seven justices.
questions.memoryHook: Seven justices in the desert - lucky seven under the Arizona sun!

questions.question: Which statement best describes gerrymandering?
questions.correctAnswer: Drawing voting district lines to favor one party
questions.explanation: Gerrymandering manipulates district boundaries for partisan advantage.
questions.memoryHook: Gerrymander is a sneaky salamander - it twists district shapes!

questions.question: Which statement best describes tribal sovereignty for Arizona tribes such as the Navajo Nation and the Tohono O'odham Nation?
questions.correctAnswer: They are self-governing nations with their own constitutions, councils, laws, and courts, keeping powers they held long before the United States existed
distractors: They are agencies of the Arizona state government
They are departments of the counties where their land lies
They are private cultural organizations with no governing powers
questions.explanation: In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831), the US Supreme Court called the tribes 'domestic dependent nations': they keep inherent powers of self-government that predate the United States. Article 1, Section 8 of the US Constitution gives Congress - not the states - the power to regulate commerce with the tribes, which is why Arizona tribes answer to federal and tribal law, not to Phoenix or to county boards.
questions.memoryHook: Tribes were governing themselves long before 1776 - sovereignty means they never gave that power up!

questions.question: Which part of Congress must approve treaties?
questions.correctAnswer: The Senate, by a two-thirds vote
questions.explanation: The President negotiates treaties, but the Senate must approve them with two-thirds support.
questions.memoryHook: Senate seals the deal - two-thirds of senators must agree!

questions.question: Which statement best describes a filibuster?
questions.correctAnswer: Extended debate used to delay or block a Senate vote
questions.explanation: Senators can speak at length to delay action; ending one requires 60 votes, called cloture.
questions.memoryHook: Filibuster is a talk-a-thon - senators talk until everyone is tired!

questions.question: Which amendment lowered the voting age to 18?
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1971, the 26th Amendment set the voting age at 18.
questions.memoryHook: 26 for 18-year-olds - old enough to be drafted, old enough to vote!

questions.question: Which action is an example of civic participation BEYOND voting?
questions.correctAnswer: Speaking during the public-comment period at a city council meeting about a proposed zoning change
distractors: Casting a ballot in a school board election
Checking your voter registration status online
questions.explanation: Voting is only one tool of citizenship. Residents also shape government by attending and speaking at council, school board, and county meetings, contacting officials, and serving on local boards. Zoning, parks, and budgets are decided in those meeting rooms - often in front of very few residents.
questions.memoryHook: Showing up and speaking up at a local meeting can move more dirt than a hundred online likes!

questions.question: How many federally recognized tribes are located in Arizona?
questions.explanation: Twenty-two federally recognized tribal nations are based in Arizona, including the Navajo Nation, the Hopi Tribe, the Tohono O'odham Nation, the Gila River Indian Community, and the San Carlos Apache Tribe. Together their lands cover more than a quarter of the state's area - one of the largest tribal land shares of any state.
questions.memoryHook: 22 tribal nations call Arizona home - their lands cover more than a quarter of the whole state!

questions.question: How can the US Constitution be amended?
questions.correctAnswer: Proposed by two-thirds of Congress or a convention, then ratified by three-fourths of the states
distractors: By a simple majority of voters
questions.explanation: Article V sets a high bar: two-thirds to propose, three-fourths of states to ratify.
questions.memoryHook: Amending is hard - two-thirds to propose, three-fourths to approve!

questions.question: Which statement best describes judicial review?
questions.correctAnswer: The power of courts to declare laws unconstitutional
questions.explanation: Established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), courts can strike down laws that violate the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: Courts review the rules - if a law breaks the Constitution, courts break the law!

questions.question: Which Supreme Court case established judicial review?
questions.explanation: In 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion in Marbury v. Madison claimed the power of judicial review.
questions.memoryHook: Marbury made it - 1803, the year courts got their superpower!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the 'supremacy clause'?
questions.correctAnswer: The part of the Constitution saying federal law beats conflicting state law
distractors: A rule about the President's power
questions.explanation: Article VI's supremacy clause makes the Constitution and federal laws the supreme law of the land.
questions.memoryHook: Supreme means top dog - federal law wins every fight!

questions.question: Under Article 21 of the Arizona Constitution, what must happen before a proposed amendment can become part of the constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: A majority of Arizona voters must approve it at an election
distractors: The governor must sign it, like a regular bill
Two-thirds of the legislature must pass it twice, with no vote of the people
The Arizona Supreme Court must approve its wording
questions.explanation: Article 21, Section 1 allows an amendment to be proposed by a majority of the members of each house of the legislature, or by an initiative petition signed by electors equal to 15 percent of the votes cast for governor. Either way, it becomes part of the constitution only if a majority of voters approve it - the governor's signature plays no role. That easy path is one reason the Arizona Constitution has been amended more than 150 times, while the US Constitution has just 27 amendments.
questions.memoryHook: In Arizona the people hold the pen - no amendment counts until the voters say yes!

questions.question: What vote is required in the Senate to convict in an impeachment trial?
questions.explanation: After the House impeaches, the Senate holds a trial and needs two-thirds to convict and remove.
questions.memoryHook: Two-thirds to remove - it takes a supermajority to fire a President!

questions.question: Which amendment covers rights kept by the people even though they are not listed?
questions.explanation: The 9th Amendment says listing some rights does not deny others the people still hold.
questions.memoryHook: Nine keeps the rest - rights not listed are still yours!

questions.question: What are 'enumerated powers'?
questions.correctAnswer: Powers specifically listed for Congress in the Constitution
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 8 lists Congress's enumerated powers like coining money and declaring war.
questions.memoryHook: Enumerated means numbered - powers listed one by one!

questions.question: What are 'implied powers'?
questions.correctAnswer: Powers Congress has that are not listed but are needed to carry out its listed powers
questions.explanation: The Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress use means not listed to execute its enumerated powers.
questions.memoryHook: Implied is hinted - not written, but understood!

questions.question: Why can Arizona not simply enforce its own laws and taxes on tribal lands inside the state's borders?
questions.correctAnswer: Tribes are sovereign governments, so state power in Indian country is limited by the US Constitution and federal law; shared issues are handled through negotiated agreements such as gaming compacts
distractors: The Arizona Constitution forbids the state from ever making agreements with tribes
Arizona could enforce state law there at any time, but chooses not to
Tribal lands are owned and governed directly by the Bureau of Indian Affairs
questions.explanation: Because tribes are sovereign and the US Constitution assigns tribal affairs to Congress, state laws generally stop at the reservation border unless Congress says otherwise. Casino gaming shows how it works in practice: under the federal Indian Gaming Regulatory Act of 1988, tribes negotiate compacts with the state, and Arizona voters approved the standard compact model in Proposition 202 in 2002. Tribal land is held in trust for the tribes - it is governed by the tribes, not by the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
questions.memoryHook: On tribal land, tribal law rules - the state has to negotiate across the table, not dictate!

questions.question: What vote is required for Congress to propose a constitutional amendment?
questions.correctAnswer: A two-thirds vote in both houses
questions.explanation: Article V requires two-thirds of both the House and Senate to propose an amendment.
questions.memoryHook: Two-thirds to propose - proposing is easier than ratifying!

questions.question: How many states must ratify a constitutional amendment?
questions.explanation: Three-fourths of the states (38 of 50) must approve an amendment for it to take effect.
questions.memoryHook: 38 states to ratify - three-fourths says yes!

questions.question: Arizona has no lieutenant governor. Who is next in line if the governor cannot serve?
questions.explanation: Under Article 5 of the Arizona Constitution, the elected Secretary of State - who runs Arizona's elections - is first after the governor, ahead of the Attorney General, because Arizona created no lieutenant governor's office.
questions.memoryHook: No lieutenant in Arizona - the Secretary of State steps up!

questions.question: In 1911, President William Howard Taft blocked Arizona statehood over one provision of its proposed constitution. What was the provision, and what happened to it after statehood?
questions.correctAnswer: The recall of judges - voters removed it to win statehood, then restored it at the first state election in November 1912
distractors: The initiative process - Congress deleted it from the constitution permanently
Women's suffrage - voters dropped it and did not restore it for decades
Direct election of senators - the legislature refused to change it
questions.explanation: Taft vetoed the statehood resolution in August 1911 mainly because the constitution let voters recall judges, part of the recall system in Article 8. Arizona voters removed judges from the recall in December 1911, statehood followed on February 14, 1912 - and at the first state election, on November 5, 1912, voters restored judicial recall by a wide margin, 16,272 to 3,705.
questions.memoryHook: Taft said 'no recalling judges' - Arizona said 'fine, for now,' became a state, and put it right back in 1912!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the difference between civil and criminal law?
questions.correctAnswer: Criminal law punishes offenses against society; civil law resolves disputes between people
distractors: Civil law is federal and criminal law is state
questions.explanation: Criminal cases are brought by the government and can lead to jail; civil cases seek money or orders between parties.
questions.memoryHook: Criminal means crime time - civil means let us settle this nicely!

questions.question: Which statement best describes double jeopardy?
questions.correctAnswer: You cannot be tried twice for the same crime
questions.explanation: The 5th Amendment bars being put in jeopardy twice for the same offense.
questions.memoryHook: Double jeopardy is double trouble - one trial per crime, that is the rule!

questions.question: Which statement best describes how the Navajo Nation, the largest tribal nation in Arizona, is governed?
questions.correctAnswer: By a popularly elected president and the Navajo Nation Council, based in the capital at Window Rock
distractors: By a governor appointed by the President of the United States
By the Arizona legislature, which passes its laws
By the Hopi Tribal Council, which governs all of northern Arizona
questions.explanation: The Navajo Nation governs itself from Window Rock, Arizona, through a president elected by Navajo voters and a legislative Navajo Nation Council of 24 delegates. Its reservation is the largest in the United States, stretching across Arizona, Utah, and New Mexico. The Hopi Tribe is a separate sovereign nation, entirely surrounded by Navajo land but not governed by it.
questions.memoryHook: Window Rock is a capital just like Phoenix - the Navajo president and council run a real government there!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the 'full faith and credit' clause?
questions.correctAnswer: States must honor other states' public acts and court decisions
questions.explanation: Article IV requires each state to honor the public acts, records, and court judgments of the others, so a marriage license or court judgment from one state is recognized in Arizona.
questions.memoryHook: Full faith means full trust - states trust each other's paperwork!

questions.question: Which statement best describes a 'writ of habeas corpus'?
questions.correctAnswer: A court order requiring a prisoner to be brought before a judge
questions.explanation: It protects against unlawful detention by forcing the government to justify holding someone.
questions.memoryHook: Habeas corpus means produce the body - show the prisoner or set them free!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Arizona Corporation Commission?
questions.correctAnswer: The state body that regulates utilities and corporations
questions.explanation: Arizona's Corporation Commission oversees public utilities, securities, and corporate filings.
questions.memoryHook: The Corporation Commission corrals corporations - keeping utilities honest in the desert!

questions.question: Which statement best describes 'selective incorporation'?
questions.correctAnswer: Applying most Bill of Rights protections to the states through the 14th Amendment
distractors: Choosing which states join the Union
questions.explanation: The 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause has been used to apply nearly all Bill of Rights limits to state governments too.
questions.memoryHook: Selective incorporation picks protections - the 14th Amendment shares the Bill of Rights with the states!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the 'establishment clause'?
questions.correctAnswer: The 1st Amendment ban on government establishing a religion
questions.explanation: The 1st Amendment says Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion.
questions.memoryHook: Establishment is a no-go - government cannot pick a favorite religion!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the 'free exercise clause'?
questions.correctAnswer: The 1st Amendment protection of practicing religion freely
questions.explanation: Alongside the establishment clause, it bars government from blocking religious practice.
questions.memoryHook: Free exercise means practice freely - worship however you wish!

questions.question: The Declaration of Independence says governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed.' How did that idea shape the US Constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: It grounded the Constitution in popular sovereignty - 'We the People' establish it, and officials hold power only through the people's continuing consent, renewed in elections
distractors: It required every federal law to be approved in a nationwide popular vote
It gave the Supreme Court the power to strike down any law the people dislike
It limited voting rights to property owners who consented in writing
questions.explanation: Jefferson's 1776 phrase became the Constitution's operating principle in 1787: the Preamble opens 'We the People... do ordain and establish this Constitution,' claiming authority from the people rather than from a king or from the states alone. Regular elections, the amendment process, and - in Arizona - the initiative, referendum, and recall are the machinery that keeps that consent current.
questions.memoryHook: No consent, no power - that 1776 idea is the engine humming under the whole Constitution!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the 'Miranda' rule?
questions.correctAnswer: Police must inform suspects of their rights before questioning
questions.explanation: From Miranda v. Arizona (1966), suspects must be told of the right to remain silent and to have a lawyer.
questions.memoryHook: Miranda means rights - you have the right to remain silent, even in Arizona!

questions.question: Which statement best describes a 'pocket veto'?
questions.correctAnswer: When the President lets a bill die by not signing it after Congress adjourns
questions.explanation: If Congress adjourns within 10 days and the President does not sign, the bill dies without a veto Congress can override.
questions.memoryHook: Pocket veto hides the bill - the President pockets it and walks away!

questions.question: Which statement best describes 'cloture'?
questions.correctAnswer: The Senate procedure to end debate, requiring 60 votes
questions.explanation: Cloture stops a filibuster; 60 senators must agree to move to a vote.
questions.memoryHook: Cloture closes the talk - 60 votes to stop the chatter!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the 'commerce clause' and why does it matter?
questions.correctAnswer: It lets Congress regulate interstate commerce, the basis for much federal power
questions.explanation: Article I's commerce clause has been read broadly to support federal laws on everything from civil rights to the environment.
questions.memoryHook: Commerce crosses borders - Congress regulates trade between states!

questions.question: Which statement best describes 'federalism'?
questions.correctAnswer: The division of power between national and state governments
questions.explanation: Federalism splits sovereignty so both levels govern in their own spheres.
questions.memoryHook: Federalism is a power split - like sharing a pizza between D.C. and Phoenix!

questions.question: What does Arizona's Voter Protection Act do?
questions.correctAnswer: It bars the legislature from repealing voter-approved initiatives
questions.explanation: The Voter Protection Act (Proposition 105, 1998) bars the legislature from repealing a voter-approved initiative; it may amend one only by a three-fourths vote, and only if the change furthers the measure's purpose.
questions.memoryHook: Voters protect their votes - the legislature cannot undo what voters approved!

questions.question: How are Arizona Supreme Court justices selected?
questions.correctAnswer: Merit selection: a commission nominates, the governor appoints, voters decide retention
questions.explanation: Arizona uses merit selection plus retention elections to balance independence and accountability.
questions.memoryHook: Merit picks the best - commission, governor, then voters give a thumbs up!

questions.question: Which statement best describes a 'retention election'?
questions.correctAnswer: Voters decide yes or no on keeping a judge in office
questions.explanation: Merit-selected Arizona judges - appellate judges and superior court judges in large counties - face yes-or-no retention votes instead of running against an opponent.
questions.memoryHook: Retention means keep or cut - voters give judges a report card!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission?
questions.correctAnswer: The citizen commission that draws congressional and legislative districts
questions.explanation: Voters created it in 2000 to take map-drawing out of partisan hands.
questions.memoryHook: Independent maps, fair districts - citizens draw the lines, not politicians!

questions.question: Which of these is a legal responsibility of US citizenship - something a citizen can actually be required to do - that does NOT involve voting?
questions.correctAnswer: Serving on a jury when summoned by a court
distractors: Paying a poll tax before taking part in an election
Attending every meeting of the city council
questions.explanation: Jury service is a duty a court can compel: when a summons arrives, a citizen must appear unless excused. It matters because the Sixth and Seventh Amendments promise trial by jury - a promise that only works if ordinary citizens serve. Joining a party and attending meetings are free choices, and the poll tax was banned by the Twenty-fourth Amendment and court decisions.
questions.memoryHook: A jury summons is not junk mail - it is the Bill of Rights asking you to report for duty!

questions.question: Which statement best describes 'civic virtue' and why did the Framers value it?
questions.correctAnswer: Citizens putting the common good first; republics depend on it
questions.explanation: The Framers believed self-government only works if citizens participate responsibly and honestly.
questions.memoryHook: Civic virtue is giant responsibility - the republic needs good citizens to survive!
